title: Systemic Infectious Diseases
subject: Immune System (IMMU)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter covers the classic systemic infections of childhood and young adulthood: the rash illnesses (measles, rubella, erythema infectiosum, roseola, scarlet fever), Haemophilus influenzae type b, influenza, mumps, Epstein-Barr virus and cytomegalovirus mononucleosis, and toxoplasmosis. Board questions give an age, a rash pattern, and a timeline, then ask for the organism and the complication most likely in a particular host. Nearly every complication here follows from three questions: which cell the organism infects, which arm of immunity controls it, and what happens when that host is pregnant, has a short red cell lifespan, or has lost T cell immunity.
prerequisites: Structure and replication of DNA and RNA viruses, enveloped and nonenveloped
T-independent versus T-dependent antibody responses and the role of the spleen
Cell-mediated immunity: Th1 cells, IFN-gamma, macrophage activation, and CD8 cytotoxic T cells
Erythropoiesis, reticulocytes, and red cell lifespan

connections.how: Parvovirus B19 halts erythropoiesis and EBV triggers cold agglutinin hemolysis, so red cell kinetics explain who becomes anemic.
Group A streptococcal pharyngitis leads to rheumatic heart disease and poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis through two different hypersensitivity mechanisms.
Rubella, CMV, Toxoplasma, and parvovirus B19 cross the placenta, and the organs damaged depend on what is forming at the time of infection.
Loss of T cell surveillance reactivates latent CMV, EBV, and Toxoplasma, producing retinitis, lymphoma, and ring-enhancing brain lesions.
EBV latent proteins drive B cell proliferation and block apoptosis, linking a common infection to Burkitt lymphoma, Hodgkin lymphoma, and nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

sections.title: Parvovirus B19: erythema infectiosum, aplastic crisis, and hydrops fetalis

blocks.text: Parvovirus B19 is a small, nonenveloped, single-stranded DNA virus spread mainly by respiratory droplets, and less often by blood products and across the placenta. Its receptor is the P antigen (globoside), which is dense on erythroid progenitors, so the virus replicates in and kills pronormoblasts in the marrow. During viremia, about one week after exposure, red cell production stops for about 7 to 10 days. With a normal red cell lifespan of about 120 days, that pause lowers hemoglobin only slightly and goes unnoticed.

In school-age children the illness is erythema infectiosum (fifth disease). A mild, flu-like prodrome accompanies the viremia. About one to two weeks later, as IgM and IgG appear, bright red cheeks with relative sparing around the mouth (slapped cheek) are followed by a lacy, reticular rash on the extensor limbs and trunk that can fade and return for weeks with heat, sunlight, or exercise. The rash and joint symptoms are produced by immune complexes, so by the time the rash appears the child is no longer viremic or contagious. Adults, especially women, more often develop symmetric arthralgia or arthritis of the hands, wrists, and knees, frequently without the rash.
Why some hosts become severely anemic

The same one-week pause in production becomes dangerous whenever red cells survive only briefly or demand is very high. In sickle cell disease or hereditary spherocytosis, red cells may last only 10 to 20 days, so hemoglobin falls sharply over a few days. The clue is a reticulocyte count near zero, the opposite of the high count expected in hemolysis, and the marrow shows giant pronormoblasts with intranuclear inclusions. A fetus has a rapidly expanding red cell mass and shorter red cell survival, and the virus can also infect fetal myocardium, so severe anemia leads to high-output heart failure and hydrops fetalis, with the greatest risk after maternal infection in the first half of pregnancy.

sections.title: Haemophilus influenzae: invasive type b disease and nontypeable mucosal infection

blocks.text: Haemophilus influenzae is a small gram-negative coccobacillus that colonizes the nasopharynx and spreads by respiratory droplets. It needs factor X (hemin) and factor V (NAD) to grow, which is why it grows on chocolate agar or around Staphylococcus aureus colonies on blood agar. Strains with a capsule are typed a to f, and the type b capsule, polyribosylribitol phosphate (PRP), is the key virulence factor: it blocks complement deposition and phagocytosis, letting the organism survive in blood and seed the meninges, epiglottis, joints, and lungs. An IgA protease helps all strains colonize mucosa.

Clearing an encapsulated organism requires anticapsular antibody that opsonizes it, followed by removal in the spleen. Maternal IgG protects for the first few months. Children younger than about 2 years respond poorly to T-independent polysaccharide antigens, so between roughly 3 months and 3 years they had little anti-PRP antibody and invasive Hib disease peaked. The conjugate vaccine links PRP to a protein carrier, which recruits T cell help, class switching, and memory even in infants. Invasive Hib disease is now seen mainly in unvaccinated or incompletely vaccinated children and in people with asplenia or antibody or complement deficiency.
Invasive syndromes

Epiglottitis is cellulitis of the supraglottic tissues. The swollen epiglottis narrows the laryngeal inlet, an extrathoracic site, so obstruction is worst during inspiration, when airway pressure falls below atmospheric pressure, producing inspiratory stridor. The child has abrupt high fever and looks toxic, drools because swallowing is painful, has a muffled voice, and sits upright, leaning forward on the hands with the chin thrust up (tripod position), to hold the airway open. A lateral neck film shows a swollen epiglottis (thumb sign). Croup, usually caused by parainfluenza virus, differs by gradual onset, low fever, barking cough, and subglottic narrowing (steeple sign). Before vaccination Hib was also a leading cause of bacterial meningitis in young children, often leaving sensorineural hearing loss, and caused bacteremia, pneumonia, septic arthritis, and facial cellulitis.

blocks.title: Type b versus nontypeable H influenzae
rows: Hematogenous to meninges, epiglottis, joints, lungs
Contiguous from nasopharynx to nearby mucosa
Epiglottitis, meningitis, bacteremia, pneumonia, septic arthritis
Otitis media, sinusitis, conjunctivitis, bronchitis and COPD exacerbations
Children of any vaccine status; adults with chronic lung disease
blocks.caption: The capsule decides whether the organism invades the blood or stays on mucosal surfaces.

blocks.text: Nontypeable strains lack a capsule, so complement and phagocytes clear them from blood easily. They therefore cause disease by spreading along mucosal surfaces from the nasopharynx into the middle ear, sinuses, conjunctiva, and lower airways, where obstruction of drainage or damaged mucociliary clearance lets them persist. Because the vaccine induces only anti-PRP antibody, these infections remain common in fully vaccinated children.

Influenza virus is an orthomyxovirus: enveloped, with a genome of eight segments of negative-sense RNA. Hemagglutinin binds sialic acid on respiratory epithelium and mediates fusion inside the endosome, and neuraminidase cleaves sialic acid so new virions can leave the cell and pass through mucus. Point mutations in these two genes (antigenic drift) cause yearly epidemics, while reassortment of whole segments between human and animal strains (antigenic shift), which occurs only in influenza A, produces pandemics.

After an incubation of about 1 to 4 days, illness begins abruptly with fever, often 38 to 40 °C (100.4 to 104 °F), chills, headache, myalgia, malaise, sore throat, and a dry cough. The virus stays in the respiratory tract; the systemic symptoms come from circulating cytokines such as type I interferons, IL-6, and TNF. Fever usually lasts 3 to 5 days, but cough and fatigue can persist for weeks while the epithelium regenerates. Complications are most likely in adults over 65, children under 2, pregnant women, and people with chronic heart or lung disease or immunosuppression.

Loss of ciliated epithelium and exposed basement membrane let bacteria adhere and invade

blocks.caption: The relapse after initial improvement is the clue that separates bacterial superinfection from primary viral pneumonia.

blocks.caption: Viral injury removes the barrier; bacteria cause the second illness.

blocks.text: Reye syndrome shows why mitochondrial failure affects liver and brain together. Impaired mitochondrial beta-oxidation causes microvesicular fatty change in hepatocytes and hypoglycemia, and loss of the mitochondrial urea cycle enzymes raises blood ammonia. Aminotransferases rise while bilirubin stays normal or only mildly raised. Ammonia is taken up by astrocytes and converted to glutamine, which swells them and produces cerebral edema and raised intracranial pressure without inflammation in the brain. The syndrome became rare once aspirin was no longer given to febrile children.

sections.title: Measles: prodrome, rash, immune suppression, and complications

blocks.text: Measles (rubeola) virus is a paramyxovirus: enveloped, with nonsegmented negative-sense RNA. It is among the most contagious human pathogens, spreading by airborne droplets to about 90% of susceptible contacts. Its H protein binds CD150 (SLAM) on activated lymphocytes, dendritic cells, and macrophages, and nectin-4 on airway epithelium; its F protein fuses cells into multinucleated giant cells. The virus travels from airway immune cells to lymph nodes, spreads by viremia to skin, conjunctiva, and respiratory and gut mucosa, and is shed through the epithelium.

After about 10 to 14 days of incubation, a 2 to 4 day prodrome brings high fever and the three Cs: cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis with photophobia. Koplik spots, small bluish-white spots on a red base on the buccal mucosa opposite the molars, appear 1 to 2 days before the rash and are pathognomonic. The maculopapular rash begins at the hairline and behind the ears, spreads down over about 3 days, becomes confluent on the face and upper body, and fades in the same order with brownish staining and fine scaling. Fever peaks with the rash and the child looks ill. The rash reflects CD8 T cells attacking infected cells in dermal capillaries, so in severe T cell deficiency it may be absent while a fatal giant cell pneumonia progresses.

Because the virus infects and kills memory lymphocytes, measles causes lymphopenia, loss of tuberculin skin reactivity, and a prolonged loss of existing immunity (immune amnesia). This explains why bacterial superinfections and other infections follow measles for weeks to months. Lymphoid tissue shows Warthin-Finkeldey multinucleated giant cells.

blocks.title: Complications of measles
rows: During or soon after the rash
Most common cause of measles death; viral giant cell pneumonia or secondary bacterial pneumonia
Within about 2 weeks of the rash; about 1 per 1,000 cases
Mostly postinfectious autoimmune demyelination (acute disseminated encephalomyelitis); fever, seizures, altered consciousness; often leaves deficits
Persistent defective virus (faulty M protein) spreads between neurons; cognitive decline, myoclonus, death; high anti-measles antibody in CSF; risk higher after infection before age 2
blocks.caption: Respiratory complications kill most patients; the neurologic complications differ by timing and mechanism.

blocks.text: Vitamin A, as retinoic acid, is needed to maintain differentiated respiratory, intestinal, and corneal epithelium and for normal mucosal immune responses. Measles consumes body stores of vitamin A, and children who start deficient have more severe pneumonia and diarrhea, corneal ulceration progressing to blindness, and higher mortality. This is why measles deaths are concentrated in malnourished children.

sections.title: Infectious mononucleosis: EBV, atypical lymphocytes, and heterophile antibodies

blocks.text: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV, human herpesvirus 4) is an enveloped double-stranded DNA gammaherpesvirus spread in saliva. It infects oropharyngeal epithelium and B lymphocytes: its glycoprotein gp350 binds CD21 (complement receptor 2) on B cells, and MHC class II serves as a coreceptor. Infected B cells proliferate and spread through lymphoid tissue. Most infections in young children are silent, but a first infection in an adolescent or young adult (about 15 to 24 years) usually causes infectious mononucleosis after an incubation of about 4 to 6 weeks. The symptoms come mainly from the vigorous T cell response, which is why they are worse in older patients.

The classic patient has fever, marked fatigue, sore throat with enlarged, often exudative tonsils, and lymphadenopathy that includes the posterior cervical chain (strep pharyngitis usually involves only anterior nodes). Splenomegaly occurs in about half, from lymphoid hyperplasia, and palatal petechiae and mild hepatomegaly are common.

Blood shows an absolute lymphocytosis with atypical lymphocytes, usually more than 10% of lymphocytes. These are mainly activated CD8 T cells killing infected B cells: large cells with abundant pale blue cytoplasm that scallops around neighboring red cells. They are not infected B cells. Heterophile antibodies are IgM made by polyclonally activated B cells; they agglutinate sheep or horse red cells (the basis of the Monospot test) but do not recognize EBV.

blocks.title: Laboratory evidence of EBV infection
rows: Supportive; also seen in CMV, acute HIV, toxoplasmosis
Polyclonal IgM against sheep or horse red cells
Positive in about 85% of adolescents and adults; often negative in the first week and in children under 4
Appears weeks to months later; its presence argues against acute infection
blocks.caption: A negative heterophile test early in illness or in a young child does not exclude EBV.

blocks.text: When an adolescent with EBV pharyngitis is thought to have strep throat and receives amoxicillin or ampicillin, a generalized, itchy maculopapular rash commonly appears within several days to about a week of starting the drug. It is thought to be an immune reaction to the drug in the setting of intense B and T cell activation, and it usually does not indicate a lasting penicillin allergy.

blocks.predict: A 17-year-old with 3 days of fever, exudative pharyngitis, posterior cervical nodes, and atypical lymphocytes has a negative Monospot. Does this exclude EBV?
blocks.explain: No. Heterophile IgM takes time to rise and is often negative in the first week; repeat testing or anti-VCA IgM would answer the question.

sections.title: Complications of EBV: spleen, liver, blood, and cancer

blocks.text: The acute complications follow from lymphocyte infiltration of organs. In the spleen, lymphocytes expand the red pulp and infiltrate the thin capsule and trabeculae, so an enlarged spleen is also a fragile one. Rupture is rare (well under 1% of cases), occurs mostly in the first 3 weeks, and can follow minor trauma or happen spontaneously, with left upper quadrant pain, pain referred to the left shoulder from blood irritating the diaphragm, and hypotension. Mild hepatitis with raised aminotransferases is present in most patients, from portal lymphocytic infiltration rather than direct killing of hepatocytes, and jaundice is uncommon.

Blood complications come from immune dysregulation. Polyclonal B cell activation can produce cold agglutinins, IgM with anti-i specificity that binds red cells in cool peripheral vessels and fixes complement, causing usually mild, transient autoimmune hemolytic anemia. Thrombocytopenia and neutropenia also occur. Massive tonsillar enlargement can obstruct the airway. Boys with X-linked lymphoproliferative disease (defective SAP protein) cannot control the T cell response and may die of uncontrolled lymphoproliferation and hemophagocytosis.
How EBV causes cancer

After primary infection EBV stays latent for life in memory B cells. Latent proteins keep infected cells alive: EBNA-1 maintains the viral episome, EBNA-2 activates host genes including MYC, and LMP-1 acts like a permanently activated CD40 receptor, driving NF-kappaB and anti-apoptotic proteins such as BCL-2. In a healthy host, CD8 T cells kill cells that express these proteins. Cancer emerges when that surveillance fails, as in transplant recipients and people with AIDS, or when an additional genetic event, such as a MYC translocation, lets a cell grow while expressing few viral proteins that T cells can see.

blocks.text: EBV also causes oral hairy leukoplakia in immunosuppressed patients, a nonmalignant white, corrugated plaque on the lateral tongue from viral replication in squamous epithelium. It cannot be scraped off, which separates it from oral candidiasis.

sections.title: Mumps: parotitis and glandular and neural spread

blocks.text: Mumps virus is a paramyxovirus: enveloped, with nonsegmented negative-sense RNA and two surface glycoproteins, hemagglutinin-neuraminidase (HN) and fusion (F) protein. It spreads by respiratory droplets and saliva, with an incubation of about 16 to 18 days. The virus replicates in upper airway epithelium and regional lymph nodes, then a viremia seeds glandular tissue (salivary glands, testes, ovaries, pancreas, breast) and the central nervous system. This shared viremia explains why parotitis, orchitis, pancreatitis, and meningitis are parts of one infection and why any of them can occur without parotid swelling.

After a short prodrome of low fever and malaise, one or both parotid glands swell and become tender, often one after the other, obscuring the angle of the mandible and pushing the earlobe up and out. The parotid is enclosed in a tight fascial capsule, so swelling is painful, and chewing or sour foods, which stimulate saliva secretion, worsen the pain. The opening of the parotid duct opposite the upper second molar may be red. Patients are contagious from a few days before to about 5 days after the swelling begins.

Lower abdominal pain or breast tenderness
Headache, neck stiffness; CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis with negative Gram stain

blocks.caption: Viremia carries the virus to every gland and to the meninges, so complications can appear without parotitis.

blocks.text: Amylase and lipase

Serum amylase comes from two sources: salivary (S-type) amylase from the salivary glands and pancreatic (P-type) amylase from the pancreas. An inflamed parotid leaks S-type amylase into the blood, so total serum amylase rises with parotitis alone. Lipase is made almost entirely by the pancreas, so a raised lipase, or a rise in the pancreatic amylase fraction, is what indicates mumps pancreatitis. A high amylase in a child with parotid swelling is therefore expected and does not by itself prove pancreatic involvement.

sections.title: Roseola infantum: fever first, rash after

blocks.text: Roseola infantum (exanthem subitum, sixth disease) is the primary infection with human herpesvirus 6, mainly the HHV-6B variant, and less often HHV-7. Both are enveloped double-stranded DNA betaherpesviruses, the same subfamily as CMV. They infect CD4 T lymphocytes (HHV-7 uses CD4 itself as its receptor), establish lifelong latency in monocytes and macrophages, and are shed in the saliva of healthy older children and adults. Maternal IgG protects for the first months, so infection occurs mostly between about 6 months and 2 years, and nearly all children are infected by age 3.

The illness begins with an abrupt high fever, often 39 to 40 °C (102.2 to 104 °F), that lasts 3 to 5 days in a child who usually looks surprisingly well, sometimes with mild upper respiratory symptoms, cervical lymphadenopathy, or a bulging fontanelle. The fever then ends abruptly. Within hours to a day, small rose-pink, blanching macules and papules appear on the trunk and spread to the neck, face, and limbs. The rash does not itch and fades in 1 to 2 days. The rash is thought to reflect the immune response as viremia is cleared, which is why it follows the fever instead of accompanying it.

Febrile seizures are the most important complication. Primary HHV-6 infection is one of the most common identified causes of febrile seizures in children under 2. Seizures occur during the febrile phase, before any rash, because high fever lowers the seizure threshold of the immature brain, and HHV-6 itself is neurotropic and is often found in the CSF. These seizures are usually generalized and brief. Encephalitis is rare in children; in stem cell transplant recipients, reactivated HHV-6 can cause encephalitis and marrow suppression.

3 to 5 days, high, child appears well
Appears as the fever breaks; trunk first, then neck, face, limbs
High fever in an immature brain; neurotropic virus
blocks.caption: Rash after defervescence separates roseola from measles and scarlet fever, in which the child is still febrile when the rash appears.

blocks.text: Rubella virus is an enveloped, positive-sense, single-stranded RNA virus, classically grouped with the togaviruses. It spreads by respiratory droplets, has an incubation of about 14 to 21 days, replicates in the nasopharynx and regional lymph nodes, and then spreads by viremia. Patients shed virus from about a week before to a week after the rash, and up to half of infections cause no symptoms.

Tender postauricular, suboccipital, and posterior cervical lymphadenopathy often appears before the rash, reflecting viral replication in those nodes. A low fever and mild malaise accompany a pink, discrete maculopapular rash that starts on the face, spreads to the trunk and limbs within a day, and fades in about 3 days. Unlike the measles rash, it does not become confluent or leave brown staining, and the child looks well. Adults, especially women, often develop arthralgia or arthritis of the fingers, wrists, and knees, attributed to immune complexes, which can last for weeks.
Congenital rubella

When a nonimmune woman acquires rubella in pregnancy, the virus crosses the placenta and causes a chronic infection of fetal tissues. It slows cell division, triggers apoptosis, and damages vascular endothelium during organogenesis, so the organs forming at the time of infection are affected and the infant is small for gestational age. The risk of defects is highest with infection in the first 12 weeks and becomes low after about 16 to 20 weeks. Affected infants shed virus in urine and nasopharyngeal secretions for months, and rubella-specific IgM in the newborn proves fetal infection, because maternal IgM does not cross the placenta.

blocks.title: Congenital rubella syndrome
rows: Sensorineural deafness, the most common single defect
Persistent infection of the developing lens and retina
Patent ductus arteriosus, pulmonary artery stenosis
Microcephaly, intellectual disability, growth restriction, hepatosplenomegaly
Reduced cell division and chronic infection
blocks.caption: The classic triad is cataracts, sensorineural deafness, and patent ductus arteriosus after first-trimester infection.

sections.title: Scarlet fever and the nonsuppurative sequelae of group A streptococcus

blocks.text: Streptococcus pyogenes (group A streptococcus) is a gram-positive coccus in chains that is beta-hemolytic, catalase negative, and bacitracin sensitive. Scarlet fever is streptococcal pharyngitis, or less often a skin or wound infection, caused by a strain that makes streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxins (classically SpeA and SpeC, also called erythrogenic toxins), whose genes are carried by a bacteriophage. These toxins act as superantigens and cause diffuse capillary dilation in the skin. It is most common between about 5 and 15 years of age.

Fever and sore throat with exudative tonsillitis, tender anterior cervical nodes, and palatal petechiae come first, and the rash appears within 12 to 48 hours. It is diffuse, blanching erythema with fine papules that give a sandpaper feel, starting on the neck, axillae, and groin and generalizing within a day while sparing the palms and soles. The cheeks are flushed with circumoral pallor, and Pastia lines are linear petechial streaks in skin creases such as the antecubital fossa, where fragile capillaries leak. The tongue first has a white coat with red papillae, then the coat peels to leave a red strawberry tongue. About a week after the rash fades, the skin desquamates, most visibly on the fingertips, palms, and soles.
Rheumatic fever and glomerulonephritis

These sequelae are not caused by bacteria in the heart or kidney but by the immune response to the preceding infection, so they appear after a latent period. Rheumatic fever follows only pharyngitis: antibodies and T cells against the streptococcal M protein cross-react with cardiac myosin, valve tissue, joints, and basal ganglia neurons. Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis follows either throat or skin infection with nephritogenic strains, whose antigens form immune complexes in glomeruli that activate complement and lower serum C3.

Carditis (mitral valve most often), migratory polyarthritis, Sydenham chorea, erythema marginatum, subcutaneous nodules

sections.title: Toxoplasmosis in healthy, fetal, and immunosuppressed hosts

blocks.text: Toxoplasma gondii is an obligate intracellular protozoan. Cats are the definitive host: the sexual cycle in the cat intestine releases oocysts in feces, which become infectious after 1 to 5 days in the environment. Humans are infected by swallowing these oocysts from litter, soil, or unwashed produce, by eating tissue cysts in undercooked meat such as pork or lamb, across the placenta, or through a transplanted organ.

Rapidly dividing tachyzoites invade almost any nucleated cell and spread through blood and lymph. Control depends on cell-mediated immunity: dendritic cell IL-12 drives NK cells and Th1 cells to produce IFN-gamma, which activates macrophages, and CD8 T cells kill infected cells. Under this pressure the parasite converts to slowly dividing bradyzoites inside tissue cysts in brain, retina, and skeletal and cardiac muscle, where they persist for life. Antibody limits spread but does not eliminate the cysts.

In a healthy host, about 80 to 90% of infections are silent. Symptomatic infection is a self-limited, mononucleosis-like illness with fever, fatigue, and painless cervical lymphadenopathy, often posterior cervical, with a negative heterophile test.

Congenital toxoplasmosis usually follows a primary infection during pregnancy; a woman infected before pregnancy has immunity that keeps cysts dormant and rarely transmits. Transmission becomes more likely as pregnancy advances and the placenta grows, but fetal damage is most severe with early infection. Tachyzoites cause necrotizing inflammation in the fetal brain and retina. Necrosis around the cerebral aqueduct obstructs CSF flow (hydrocephalus), necrotic foci throughout the brain calcify (diffuse intracranial calcifications), and retinal infection causes chorioretinitis, which may first appear years after birth.

In AIDS, when the CD4 count falls below about 100 cells/mm3, the IFN-gamma response fails and brain cysts reactivate. Toxoplasmic encephalitis causes headache, fever, confusion, seizures, and focal deficits. Imaging shows multiple ring-enhancing lesions with surrounding edema, typically in the basal ganglia and at the gray-white junction; the enhancing rim is inflammation and a broken blood-brain barrier around a necrotic center. Because this is reactivation, Toxoplasma IgG is almost always positive.

blocks.title: Worked example: ring-enhancing lesions in AIDS
blocks.text: A man with AIDS and a CD4 count of 40 cells/mm3 has headache and right arm weakness. MRI shows three ring-enhancing lesions in the basal ganglia and at the gray-white junction, and Toxoplasma IgG is positive. Step 1: CD4 below 100 places him at risk for both toxoplasmosis and primary CNS lymphoma. Step 2: multiple lesions in these locations favor Toxoplasma, while lymphoma is more often a single periventricular mass. Step 3: positive IgG fits reactivation of latent cysts; a negative IgG would make toxoplasmosis much less likely. Step 4: EBV DNA in the CSF would point instead to lymphoma. The best answer is toxoplasmic encephalitis.

Five questions separate these rashes: when the rash appears relative to the fever, where it starts and how it spreads, what it looks and feels like, how ill the child looks, and what the accompanying clue is. Timing reflects pathogenesis. The measles rash comes at the peak of the T cell attack on infected cells, so the child is still febrile and sick. Scarlet fever reflects toxin acting during an ongoing bacterial infection, so fever and rash also coincide. The rashes of erythema infectiosum and roseola appear as antibody clears the viremia, so the fever is over and the child is well.

blocks.text: Three pairs cause most errors. Measles and rubella both spread from head to trunk, but measles follows a severe prodrome with the three Cs and a confluent rash in a sick child, while rubella is mild with prominent posterior nodes. Roseola and measles both begin with high fever, but in roseola the rash follows defervescence. Scarlet fever differs from the viral rashes in its rough texture, the exudative pharyngitis, and the tongue and skin-fold changes. A diffuse rash that appears days after amoxicillin in a teenager with pharyngitis points instead to EBV.

blocks.title: Worked example: fever first, then rash
blocks.text: A 14-month-old has had a temperature of 40 °C (104 °F) for 4 days but has stayed alert and playful. On day 5 the fever is gone, and that evening pink blanching spots appear on his trunk and spread to his neck. Step 1: the rash appeared after the fever ended, which rules against measles and scarlet fever, in which the child is febrile when the rash appears. Step 2: there was no cough, coryza, or conjunctivitis, and no sore throat. Step 3: his age is typical for primary HHV-6 infection. The diagnosis is roseola infantum, and the complication to anticipate during the febrile phase was a febrile seizure.

sections.title: Cytomegalovirus: mononucleosis, congenital infection, and disease in immunosuppression

blocks.text: Cytomegalovirus (CMV, human herpesvirus 5) is an enveloped double-stranded DNA betaherpesvirus. It spreads through saliva, urine, genital secretions, breast milk, leukocyte-containing blood, transplanted organs, and across the placenta. It infects epithelial and endothelial cells, fibroblasts, smooth muscle, and monocytes, which is why it can damage almost any organ. It stays latent in monocytes and myeloid progenitor cells and reactivates when T cell immunity falls. Infected cells enlarge (cytomegaly) and contain a large basophilic intranuclear inclusion surrounded by a clear halo, the owl's eye appearance, often with smaller cytoplasmic inclusions.

In healthy young adults, primary CMV infection can cause a mononucleosis syndrome with prolonged fever, fatigue, atypical lymphocytes, and mildly raised aminotransferases, but with less pharyngitis and lymphadenopathy than EBV. The heterophile test is negative, because heterophile antibodies arise from polyclonal activation of EBV-infected B cells, which CMV does not cause. CMV is the most common cause of heterophile-negative mononucleosis. A similar syndrome can follow transfusion of blood from a seropositive donor, because the virus travels in donor leukocytes.

CMV is the most common congenital infection. Transmission and severe disease are most likely after a primary maternal infection, although reactivation or reinfection can also infect the fetus. About 90% of infected newborns look normal at birth, but some of them develop hearing loss later. The virus targets the rapidly dividing cells lining the fetal ventricles, so necrosis there leaves periventricular calcifications, along with microcephaly, chorioretinitis, hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, petechiae or blueberry muffin spots, and growth restriction. Congenital CMV is the leading nongenetic cause of sensorineural hearing loss in children. In transplant recipients and people with AIDS, disease follows reactivation or new infection once T cells can no longer hold the virus latent, and in transplant recipients it is most common in the first months after transplant, when immunosuppression is most intense.

integration.text: Each infection in this chapter is defined by the cell it infects and by the arm of immunity that controls it. Parvovirus B19 targets erythroid progenitors through P antigen, so its effects are read through reticulocyte counts and red cell lifespan. Hib is controlled by anticapsular antibody and the spleen, so it strikes infants who cannot yet respond to polysaccharide, and asplenic patients. EBV, CMV, HHV-6, and Toxoplasma are held latent by T cells, so the same organisms that cause a mild illness in a healthy teenager cause lymphoma, retinitis, encephalitis, or ring-enhancing brain lesions when CD4 counts fall or transplant drugs suppress T cells.

Pregnancy and immune-mediated injury tie the chapter to other disciplines. Rubella, CMV, Toxoplasma, and parvovirus B19 cross the placenta, and the damage depends on timing and target cell: organogenesis for rubella, the periventricular germinal tissue for CMV, necrotizing inflammation for Toxoplasma, and fetal erythropoiesis for parvovirus. IgM in the newborn proves fetal infection because maternal IgM does not cross the placenta. Many findings here are produced by the host response rather than the microbe itself: the rashes of measles and fifth disease, the atypical lymphocytes of mononucleosis, and the rheumatic fever and glomerulonephritis that follow streptococcal infection. These ideas are mechanisms to reason from, and real presentations overlap, so the age, timeline, and host usually decide the answer.

summary: Parvovirus B19 kills erythroid progenitors through P antigen; the one-week production pause causes aplastic crisis with reticulocytes near zero in hemolytic anemia and hydrops fetalis in the fetus, while the slapped cheek rash appears after contagiousness ends.

The PRP capsule lets Hib invade blood; children under about 2 years cannot make antibody to polysaccharide, so unvaccinated toddlers get epiglottitis and meningitis, while unencapsulated nontypeable strains cause otitis media and sinusitis.

Influenza causes abrupt systemic symptoms from cytokines; relapse after improvement means secondary S pneumoniae or S aureus pneumonia, and aspirin in a child with influenza or varicella can cause Reye syndrome (microvesicular steatosis, hyperammonemia, cerebral edema).

Measles brings the three Cs and Koplik spots before a head-to-toe confluent rash; it destroys immune memory, kills mainly through pneumonia, causes SSPE years later, and is worse with vitamin A deficiency.
EBV enters B cells through CD21; atypical lymphocytes are CD8 T cells, heterophile antibodies are polyclonal IgM that may be negative early, and amoxicillin triggers a rash.
EBV complications include splenic rupture, hepatitis, cold agglutinin hemolysis, and B cell or epithelial cancers when T cell surveillance fails or MYC is translocated.
Mumps viremia seeds glands and meninges, causing parotitis, orchitis in postpubertal males, aseptic meningitis, and pancreatitis; amylase rises with parotitis alone, while lipase marks pancreatitis.
Roseola (HHV-6) gives several days of high fever, then a truncal rash as the fever breaks, with febrile seizures during the fever.

Rubella is mild with posterior nodes, but first-trimester infection causes cataracts, deafness, PDA, and blueberry muffin rash; scarlet fever is a toxin rash with pharyngitis that can be followed by rheumatic fever (throat only) or glomerulonephritis (throat or skin).

Toxoplasma and CMV are held latent by T cells: congenital Toxoplasma gives hydrocephalus and diffuse calcifications, congenital CMV gives periventricular calcifications and hearing loss, and in AIDS they cause ring-enhancing brain lesions (CD4 below 100) and retinitis (CD4 below 50).
